item.title: LEE CARTER: Socialism means two wildly different things to Republicans and Democrats
item.description: Gallup polling shows 65% of Democrats view socialism positively, but they're describing affordable healthcare and fairness, not the Soviet Union.
item.content:encoded:
Socialism is back.

And judging by the reaction in some Republican circles, so is the Soviet Union.

There is just one problem. Americans embracing socialism may not be talking about the socialism Republicans think they’re talking about.

MAJORITY OF AMERICANS BROADLY REJECT SOCIALIST IDEOLOGY EVEN AS FAR LEFT SURGES TO POWER

And if we don’t understand that, we’re going to miss one of the most important lessons of this election.

I’m a researcher and strategist. I spend my life studying what people believe, why they believe it, and how the same words can mean wildly different things to different people.

And right now, there may be no word in American politics more misunderstood than socialism.

To many Republicans, socialism means communism. Government control. Breadlines. Moscow. A dreary existence in which everyone is equally miserable except the people running the government.

To many Democrats, it means something else entirely.

Affordable healthcare. A decent retirement. A fair shot at getting ahead. An economy where billionaires don’t get every break while everyone else gets the bill.

Same word. Different movie.

And the polling is remarkable.

SOCIALISM SURGES AMONG DEMOCRATS AS PARTY LEADERS REJECT DSA AGENDA: ‘PACK OF FOOLS’

According to Gallup, 65% of Democrats have a positive view of socialism. So do 45% of independents. Only 14% of Republicans agree.

But here’s the really interesting part.

When Gallup asked Americans what they actually liked about socialism, Democrats and independents talked about access to basic services, economic equality, and a stronger safety net.

They weren’t describing the Soviet Union.

They were describing a country where ordinary people can afford to live.

Now, that doesn’t mean socialism is simply another word for fairness. It is a real economic philosophy with real policy implications, and Americans have legitimate disagreements about what government should own, control, regulate, and provide.

But if we’re going to have that argument, shouldn’t we first make sure we’re having the same conversation?

Because right now, one side is warning about Vladimir Lenin while the other is worried about the price of lettuce.

And the lettuce is winning.

The irony of it all is that Trump messaged this before the Democrats did. He understood something fundamental about American voters in 2016.

People were angry.

LIBERAL-CITY RESIDENT HESITATES WHEN PRESSED ON BELIEFS: 'I HADN'T REALLY THOUGHT ABOUT SOCIALISM THAT WAY'

They believed the system was rigged. They believed the powerful were getting richer while everyone else was falling behind. They believed Washington had become a private club where the members took care of themselves and sent the bill to the rest of the country.

Trump promised to drain the swamp.

He promised to fight for the forgotten man and woman.

He promised to take on an establishment that had stopped listening.

It was an extraordinarily powerful message.

And now Democrats are making a strikingly similar argument about an economy that favors the wealthy, a political system that protects insiders, and ordinary Americans who can’t seem to get ahead.

The vocabulary is different. The policy prescriptions are different. But the underlying frustration sounds awfully familiar.

The swamp is still there. The rent is still due. The grocery bill is still too high.

And voters are still asking the same question.

Who’s fighting for me?

That is the question both parties should be trying to answer.

SOCIALISM'S GROWING APPEAL MEETS AN AWKWARD REALITY CHECK ON COLLEGE CAMPUS

Not whether they can attach the most frightening label to the other side.

Not whether they can win a debate about economic philosophy that most Americans haven’t had since freshman year.

But whether they can make life more affordable, opportunity more accessible, and government more accountable.

Because here’s what politicians consistently underestimate.

Voters don’t experience the economy as an ideology.

They experience it at the grocery store. At the pharmacy. When the mortgage payment comes due. When their children graduate from college with debt and move back into their childhood bedrooms.

DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE

You can tell someone they’re living under capitalism or socialism or democratic socialism.

They’re still going to want to know why a carton of eggs costs so much.

And before Republicans assume that attacking socialism is sufficient to win back voters, they might consider what those voters believe they’re supporting.

You can oppose government ownership of industry and still believe Americans deserve affordable healthcare.

You can support free enterprise and still think the economic system is tilted toward the wealthy.

You can believe deeply in capitalism and still wonder why working hard doesn’t seem to get you as far as it used to.

LIBERAL HOT SPOT RESIDENTS CAN’T AGREE ON WHAT SOCIALISM MEANS AS FAR-LEFT MOVEMENTS GAINS STEAM

These aren’t necessarily contradictions.

They’re the complicated, sometimes messy beliefs of real people.

And they are exactly why persuasion remains possible.

The lesson of this election isn’t that America has suddenly become socialist.

It isn’t that capitalism has lost.

JONATHAN TURLEY: SOCIALISM IS BACK IN STYLE AND DEMOCRATS ARE BUYING THE PITCH

And it certainly isn’t that every candidate who talks about fairness has discovered some magical formula for political success.

It’s that the argument over what fairness means, and who is delivering it, is very much alive.

And that argument cannot be won simply by shouting a word louder.

There is an important lesson here for Democrats, too.

A positive view of socialism is not a blank check for every policy proposed in its name. Americans can support a stronger safety net while remaining deeply skeptical of government bureaucracy, higher taxes, or promises that sound wonderful until someone explains how much they cost.

The label doesn’t do the work.

The idea has to.

That’s the part I hope both parties understand.

For Republicans, the challenge is to explain how their vision of free enterprise can deliver the affordability and opportunity people are demanding.

For Democrats, the challenge is to demonstrate that their promises of fairness can produce real results without creating a whole new set of problems.

Neither side gets to skip the hard part.

DEPROGRAMMED: SHE WAS ALL IN FOR SOCIALISM - UNTIL THE 'RED FLAGS' BECAME IMPOSSIBLE TO IGNORE

Because Americans aren’t asking for a lecture on economic theory.

They’re asking for a fair shot.

And here’s the irony.

The political language that helped propel Donald Trump to the White House—fighting for forgotten Americans, challenging powerful insiders, and taking on a rigged system—is now being echoed by some of the very Democrats who built their political identities opposing him.

Different messengers. Different solutions. Familiar frustration.

Perhaps the most important question coming out of this election isn’t whether America is embracing socialism.

Perhaps it’s whether either party fully understands why so many Americans feel the economy isn’t working for them.

Because you don’t defeat an idea by attacking its name. You defeat it by offering people something better.

And you don’t win lasting support by telling voters what they should be afraid of.

You earn it by giving them something to believe in.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The American people aren’t asking for a return to Moscow.

They’re asking for a country where hard work pays off, opportunity isn’t reserved for the well-connected, and getting ahead doesn’t feel like winning the lottery.

Call that fairness. Call it opportunity. Call it the American Dream.

Just don’t make the mistake of thinking that winning an argument over the word socialism means you’ve answered the people who find it appealing.

Because the next election won’t be decided in a political science classroom.

It will be decided by Americans who want to know whether their lives are getting better.

And they are going to listen to whoever has a convincing answer.

item.title: TNA's Xia Brookside spoils ceremony for Knockouts competitor, aligns herself with The Righteous
item.description: Harley Hudson was blindsided when Xia Brookside emerged as The Righteous' newest member, but a mysterious dollhouse hint from Taryn Terrell awaited.
item.content:encoded:
Total Nonstop Action Wrestling’s (TNA) "Impact" on Thursday night was supposed to be a crowning moment for Harley Hudson.

Hudson had flirted with the possibility of joining The Righteous, the duo known as Vincent and Dutch, as they set their sights on the entire TNA roster. Dutch even saved Hudson from elimination during the Call Your Shot Gauntlet at Bound for Glory last month.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

The stars seemed to be aligned for Hudson as she made her way to the ring. Vincent and Dutch asked her to recite the words they were saying, "I am righteous. For we are many. I am righteous. For we are many. … While you were making up your mind, someone else already did."

Hudson said the last line with some trepidation as she learned in that moment she wasn’t about to join the group. Dutch stepped aside and behind the brooding figure was former Knockouts world champion Xia Brookside.

Brookside attacked Hudson and hit her with a Dark Side DDT. It appeared Hudson was left by the wayside and Brookside was the newest member of The Righteous – much to the chagrin of the fans in the arena.

Hudson wasn’t finished with her night. Beaten and embarrassed, she made a phone call to her mom.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"You told me not to trust those Righteous fellas but it all sounded so convincing," Hudson was heard saying. "Well, I don’t quite know how I get myself into these situations and I actually don’t know why it’s so hard for me to make any friends out here. I just feel like no matter how hard I try, I don’t have a home out here. I just really, really don’t want to come home yet."

Feeling down and out, Hudson found someone in her corner. She hung up the phone and found a note taped to one of the trailers in the parking lot. The note read, "Play with Meeee," sealed with a kiss. She then found a dollhouse.

It was Taryn Terrell luring Hudson to her team.

Terrell is in her third stint with TNA. She initially joined The Dollhouse group in 2015. In her tenure at TNA, she’s held the TNA Knockouts Championship once and was named Knockout of the Year in 2014.

She appeared back with the company earlier this year at Sacrifice to align with ODB and Mickie James. Now, it appears she’s found Hudson to reform The Dollhouse.

item.title: Woke 3.0 is off to a hot start as singer waves Pride flag while performing national anthem during NBA game
item.description: A singer waved a small Pride flag while performing the national anthem during Golden State Warriors Pride Night, sparking fierce backlash online.
item.content:encoded:
What a week for the left. When you're hot, you're hot!

First, they absolutely wiped the floor with Republicans in the midterm elections. Just a bloodbath. I'm pretty sure Democrats now own every single congressional seat known to man, along with a few others we don't even know exist.

None of it was great, and it somehow got worse.

That's right. It was a blue tsunami on Tuesday, and a red stock market on Thursday. And I mean a reeeeeeeeeeeed stock market.

WNBA FINALS TEAMS END SEASON WITH ONE FINAL NATIONAL ANTHEM SNUB AS DREAM, VALKYRIES LEAVE COURT

Last night, we saw all the different colors on display our in San Francisco, where a gay man not only sang the national anthem before the Golden State Warriors game, but he also waved a tiny Pride flag during the song.

A tiny rainbow flag. During the national anthem. During the actual national anthem.

You wanna talk about disrespectful. This makes the WNBA nonsense from last month look like child's play.

Woke 3.0 is off to a BLAZING start:

It's just horrible. It's so embarrassing, and pathetic, and — again — disrespectful. Why? Why do this?

Yes, it was "Pride Night" at Oracle Arena because every team has to have a Pride Night. Why? I don't know, but they do. I get it. That's fine.

But "Pride Night" doesn't give you a hall pass to do whatever you want during our country's national anthem. Feel like that's off-limits to anything and everything.

There's a right way to do it, and a wrong way to do it. No in between. Waving a Pride flag while singing it is the wrong way to do it. Plain and simple.

Even the players were stunned by it. Look at them! They can't hold back their laughter. I'm sure Steve Kerr loved it. He's probably still giddy over Tuesday's election results.

While Woke 3.0 is very clearly here, sanity still prevailed online, where this gay anthem singer was absolutely crushed for pulling this move:

Why is so difficult to just ... act normal? I don't get it? Just act right. It's not asking a lot. Really, it's not.

It's asking that you don't wave your tiny Pride flag during the national anthem, and smirk about it like you're taking some big stand. You're not taking a big stand. You look like an idiot. We're all mocking you.

ATLANTA DREAM AND GOLDEN STATE VALKYRIES SKIP NATIONAL ANTHEM FOR THIRD STRAIGHT WNBA FINALS GAME

We spent two weeks monitoring the WNBA Finals just to see if anyone would stay on the court of the national anthem, which really wasn't asking a ton.

They did not.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Now, we're waving Pride flags during the anthem? Come on.

Woke 3.0 is here, folks. Strap in for a long two years.

item.title: ABC's 'The View' hosted just one conservative guest before Election Day, MRC study finds
item.description: ABC News' "The View" hosted just one conservative guest before Election Day this season, according to a Media Research Center study of its guest list.
item.content:encoded:
ABC News' "The View" hosted just one conservative guest and 21 liberal guests in the weeks leading up to Election Day, according to a new study by the conservative media watchdog Media Research Center (MRC).

The study found that from Sept. 8, the start of Season 30, through Nov. 3, "The View" invited 21 liberal guests who were either critical of President Donald Trump or the Republican Party, with Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, being the lone conservative guest.

Four of the guests classified as liberal were politicians: Gov. Andy Beshear, D-Ky.; Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz.; Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who appeared on the show the day before Election Day alongside liberal podcast host Kara Swisher.

Although a retiring Republican senator, Tillis was included in the liberal guest count due to being invited on to discuss his anti-Trump book, "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents." 

STEPHEN A SMITH DOUBLES DOWN ON TRUMP DINNER, CHALLENGES CRITICS BY ASKING, 'WHAT THE F--- ARE YOU DOING?'

Tillis has been vocal in calling for Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's firing and has publicly broken with the president over the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill. In his book, Tillis wrote that he hoped Republicans would learn from midterm losses, which he predicted when the book was released in early October.

"What I hope is that members of my party take the loss and learn something," he wrote, according to The New York Times, "specifically that putting party affiliation — or loyalty to one man — before your own conscience never turns out well in the end."

The show hosted several liberal celebrities as well, including Maisie Williams, Ethan Hawke, Chelsea Handler, Michael Douglas, Billy Crystal, Patricia "Ms. Pat" Williams-Lee, D.L. Hughley, Chandra Wilson, Busy Philipps, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Eisa Davis, Jamie Lee Curtis and Sophia Bush.

Neil deGrasse Tyson and Stephen A. Smith were among the other guests included in the study. Smith appeared on the show to discuss his recent White House meeting with Trump, a decision that drew criticism from the co-hosts. He defended his decision to attend. The ESPN host also criticized the president during the appearance.

TRUMP SPILLS DETAILS ABOUT DINNER WITH BILL MAHER, STEPHEN A SMITH AND KID ROCK AT THE WHITE HOUSE

According to the study's methodology, guests had to express liberal or conservative views during their appearances on the talk show to be counted in either category.

"If a celebrity did not discuss politics, they were not included in the count of political leanings even if they had a history of being outspoken in the past," the MRC said.

The show hosted 56 guests in total between Sept. 8 and Nov. 3, according to the study.

The daytime talk show drew scrutiny in 2025 after hosting 128 liberal guests over the course of the year and just two conservatives. In 2026, the show hosted Vice President JD Vance and Alina Habba, a former legal spokesperson for Trump. The show also had several Republican fill-in co-hosts while Alyssa Farah Griffin was on maternity leave. The fill-ins included Elisabeth Hasselbeck and Savannah Chrisley, among others.

In January 2026, the co-hosts interviewed former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, a Republican who became a fierce Trump critic.

"The View" did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

'THE VIEW' CO-HOST WARNS AGAINST VANCE INTERVIEW BECOMING 'FREE-FOR-ALL' TO SELL BOOKS

MRC President David Bozell said in a statement, "ABC has learned nothing from the FCC’s continued scrutiny. 'The View' continues to insult the intelligence of the American public by passing off pure Democratic propaganda as a ‘bona fide news program.’" 

"With 21 anti-Republican voices and a single conservative in the two months before the midterms, ABC’s political agenda could hardly be more obvious," he continued. "And ABC is hardly alone. The entire elitist media landscape deserves serious scrutiny. The Federal Communications Commission must hold ABC accountable for its abuse of the public airwaves for partisan political purposes."

The program has faced a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) investigation over the past year. ABC has responded by defending "The View" as a "bona fide news" program.

The investigation is related to the agency's crackdown on equal-time requirements for political candidates. A source at the FCC told Fox News Digital in February that the show's interview with James Talarico triggered the probe.

"'The View' has been broadcasting under a bona fide news exemption granted to it more than twenty years ago ... The Commission has taken no action over the last two decades to modify or overturn the Declaratory Ruling and there is no basis for doing so now," ABC said in a petition in May in response to the FCC's probe.

'THE VIEW' EASED UP ON POLITICAL CANDIDATE BOOKINGS AMID FCC INQUIRY, REPORT SAYS

The co-hosts interviewed Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico on Wednesday after he won his election in Texas and interviewed Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Thursday after his election victory.

Republican Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who won her re-election campaign, is going to appear on the program next week.

item.title: James Carville cautions Democrats to stay away from DEI policies after midterm victories
item.description: James Carville warns Democrats against reviving DEI and woke politics after their historic midterm victory, saying the country simply "hated it."
item.content:encoded:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville warned Democrats against reviving DEI and woke policies after dominating the midterms, arguing these policies hurt the party.

Carville spoke with a panel on Thursday’s episode of the "Politics War Room" podcast about the Democrats' midterm victories before responding to a statement from Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., declaring that "DEI is back."

"I really like him. He's a very personable man. I think these people are all wrong," Carville reacted. "They tried DEI. The country hated it. Just hated it. It cost us seats."

Carville agreed with comments from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., dismissing "Woke 1" and argued that returning to those policies would take the party in the wrong direction.

CARVILLE SAYS ONE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST'S 'LUNACY OF THE HIGHEST LEVEL' POLICY COULD HAUNT SWING-STATE DEMS

"The DEI people asked me to honor your identity above your humanity. I cannot do that. To me, you're a human being first. And if we bring this bulls--- language back, we're going to pay for it," he said.

After the 2024 presidential election, Carville warned that the "stench" of woke politics would cling to the party like a foul smell on a shirt. While he said Democrats had made progress since then, he lamented that some were returning to those policies.

"We're finally washing the stench of defund the police, communities of color, or every idiotic jacka-- academic word that [they] could think of. And we got rid of it. And AOC is right. Woke one was some crazy s---. Let's all go back and do it," he said. "Let's have progressive taxation. Let's have pluralism in America. Let's get out of Iran. Let's open rural hospitals. Okay, these are things that we can agree on."

Carville explained that he is a liberal, not a progressive, and wants to help rural Americans who may feel abandoned by the Democratic Party.

"I think rural America is the most forgotten part of America," he said, warning that his fellow Democrats need to be "talking about the problems of rural America or rural hospitals or rural education or rural libraries or anything else."

JAMES CARVILLE WARNS FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES 'TOO HARD-HEADED' TO KNOW THEY'RE UNPOPULAR

"And I think to the extent that this whole thing strikes people as another coastal people trying to impose something on the rest of the country, and the rest of the country doesn't want this, and now we're talking about bringing it back?" he warned. 

Democrat Dan Turrentine, a co-host of "The Huddle," told Fox News Digital that Democrats largely abandoned social issues leading up to the midterms and focused on the economy and tackling "corruption."

"Not a single new member from a competitive state or district ran on restoring DEI. Quite the contrary, they stayed away from relitigating settled social issues and focused like a laser beam on costs, chaos, and corruption," Turrentine wrote. "Many people on our side are considering running for president and, in an effort to create a spark, will say controversial things to select audiences. The winning candidate will be focused on a broad coalition and keep the main things the main thing."

item.title: Your old Android phone could become a walking robot
item.description: UCLA's PhoneBot turns old Android phones into the brain of a two-legged humanoid robot that walks, follows people and stands up after falling.
item.content:encoded:
Got an old Android phone collecting dust in a drawer? You might want to hang on to it. Researchers at UCLA have figured out how to turn an aging smartphone into the brain of a small walking robot. It's called PhoneBot, and it can walk on two legs, follow people and even get back up after falling face down.

The most surprising part? The researchers estimate the robot's hardware costs about $400, excluding the phone. So, that forgotten smartphone could have a pretty interesting second life. Here's how the researchers pulled it off and what it would take to build one yourself.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

GOOGLE TURNS OLD PHONES INTO CLOUD SERVERS

PhoneBot comes from UCLA's Robotics and Mechanisms Laboratory, also known as RoMeLa. The team built a miniature humanoid robot that stands about 19 inches tall and weighs roughly four pounds, including the smartphone attached to its body.

Instead of developing an expensive custom computer, researchers used technology already inside an Android phone. The robot has 13 motorized joints, with six in each leg and another that lets its upper body rotate. That extra movement allows the smartphone's camera to turn toward someone while the robot's feet stay planted.

The researchers’ goal is to make humanoid robotics more affordable for schools and research teams that cannot spend thousands of dollars on specialized machines.

Think about everything your smartphone already does. It can recognize objects through its camera and detect movement using built-in sensors. It also has enough processing power to run sophisticated software. PhoneBot puts those capabilities to work. An Android app uses the phone's motion sensors to help the robot maintain its balance. Meanwhile, the camera helps it recognize and track people. The phone also runs an artificial intelligence-powered walking controller that tells the robot how to move. Those instructions travel over Wi-Fi to a small computer inside the robot, which communicates with the motors. The smartphone has no physical electrical connection to the robot's hardware. That design makes it easier to swap phones without rewiring the machine. Researchers trained PhoneBot's walking system in computer simulations before testing it on the actual robot. They also developed a way to improve how evenly it uses both legs. As a result, PhoneBot can walk on flat surfaces and stand up from a face-down position. For something powered largely by an old smartphone, that's quite an accomplishment.

Here's something I found especially interesting. UCLA didn't need the latest expensive smartphone to make PhoneBot work. In fact, the researchers successfully tested its core functions on four different Android devices, including an Honor 9 released back in 2017. The other models included a Samsung Galaxy A16 5G and two Motorola Moto G phones from 2024 and 2025.

Researchers purchased the three prepaid models for roughly $50 to $90 each. Those were the prices reported during testing, rather than guaranteed prices today. All four phones handled the essential functions, including movement control and camera-based recognition. However, the older Honor 9 could not run one of the robot's mapping features because the required Google services were unavailable on that device in the United States. That means you cannot assume every Android phone will work. Still, the tests suggest you may not need an expensive new phone to run a capable little robot.

A WHEELED ROBOT MAY BEAT HUMANOIDS INTO YOUR HOME

Yes, at least within the limits of what UCLA has demonstrated. PhoneBot can use its smartphone camera to identify a person and adjust its movement to follow them. It can also rotate its upper body to keep someone in view. The robot supports conversational interaction, too.

However, there's an important limitation. Its current system uses a separate laptop to process speech and generate AI responses. The smartphone records your voice and plays the response through its speaker. Before you start thinking about having PhoneBot clean your house, there's something else you should know. It doesn't have arms. That means it cannot pick up your laundry or carry groceries.

Researchers also trained its walking system on flat ground, so navigating stairs and uneven surfaces remains a challenge. For now, PhoneBot is best viewed as an experimental platform. UCLA has demonstrated what it can do under research conditions, but it hasn't established that the robot can independently navigate a typical home.

If you're comfortable with electronics and robotics, PhoneBot could become a pretty interesting project. UCLA has developed it as an open-source research platform and published hardware designs and building resources. The official PhoneBot website at phonebot.dev/ provides information about the robot's design, components and assembly process. The published hardware materials are available for noncommercial use under a Creative Commons license.

There's an important distinction, though, between having the hardware plans and being able to build a fully working robot. The project website provides hardware designs and assembly resources but does not clearly offer a download for the complete Android app and trained walking software. Although UCLA describes PhoneBot as an open-source platform, anyone hoping to reproduce its capabilities should first confirm that the necessary software is available.

And there's another consideration: the $400 price tag. It's an approximate hardware cost, and it doesn't include the smartphone. Depending on what equipment you already have, you may also need access to a 3D printer and tools for assembly. Shipping and other expenses could push the total higher. You'll also need the technical skills to put everything together and configure the software. So, don't expect to download an app and watch your old phone suddenly sprout legs. There's real engineering involved.

Humanoid robots are getting a lot of attention, but building one remains expensive. Some small research models cost several thousand dollars. More advanced systems can cost considerably more. PhoneBot takes advantage of hardware that millions of people already own. By letting a smartphone handle much of the sensing and computing, researchers can avoid buying some specialized components. That helps bring the overall cost down.

The approach could also make robotics more accessible to students. Instead of requiring a large research budget, a smaller team could experiment with a relatively inexpensive walking machine. They could test new software or explore ways to improve movement without building every electronic component from scratch.

The UCLA team already has ideas for what comes next. Researchers want to improve PhoneBot's ability to handle uneven terrain and eventually give it lightweight arms. They're also exploring ways to run more conversational AI directly on the smartphone, which could reduce the need for a separate computer. Those improvements are still future goals. Even so, PhoneBot offers a promising starting point for building more affordable humanoid robots.

You probably won't see PhoneBot on store shelves anytime soon. But this research shows how much useful technology may still be inside a smartphone you've stopped using. A phone that feels outdated for daily use could still handle surprisingly demanding tasks.

If you're interested in robotics, PhoneBot could eventually offer a more affordable way to experiment with walking machines. Meanwhile, for families with kids who love technology, an accessible version of this project could make for a fascinating hands-on learning experience.

And if you've been thinking about getting rid of your old Android phone, this research offers another reason to consider what it might still be capable of. Of course, building a robot won't be for everyone. You can also sell, donate or recycle your old phone. Before you do, check out our article on securely getting rid of your old cell phone to make sure your personal information doesn't go along with it.

I love the idea that a smartphone sitting forgotten in a drawer could become the brain of a walking robot. We've gotten so used to replacing our phones every few years that we sometimes overlook how powerful these devices still are. What UCLA has done with PhoneBot makes me wonder how many other uses we're missing. Now, let's be realistic. This little guy isn't ready to take over household chores, and putting one together requires some serious know-how. But the price is what caught my attention. When researchers can build a walking robot with roughly $400 in additional hardware, it opens the door to possibilities that once seemed out of reach. I'd love to see someone turn this into an affordable kit that families could build together. That could be a great way to get kids excited about engineering.

Would you spend a few hundred dollars to turn your old Android phone into a walking robot? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: Cannonballs unearthed at Alamo nearly 200 years after deadly siege, yet mystery remains
item.description: Four solid cannonballs unearthed near Alamo Church mark the first such artifacts found at the historic San Antonio site in Texas from the 1836 battle. An expert spoke with Fox News Digital.
item.content:encoded:
Archaeologists in San Antonio, Texas, have announced the discovery of four solid cannonballs from the Battle of the Alamo — each offering new physical evidence of the historic battle.

The discovery, made along the perimeter of Alamo Church in San Antonio, was announced in late October.

Officials from the Alamo Trust said the cannonballs were uncovered during ongoing archaeological excavations at the site, and that they "help us remember those individuals that were living here, during the battle," said Tiffany Lindley, head archaeologist at the Alamo Trust. 

HIDDEN REVOLUTIONARY WAR BAKE HOUSE IS UNCOVERED AFTER SPENDING CENTURIES UNDERGROUND

The four solid-shot cannonballs vary in size, with the smallest measuring 1.8 inches in diameter and the largest measuring 3.26 inches. 

The measurements correspond to 1-pounder and 6-pounder cannons, respectively.

The discovery follows two other finds made earlier this year: a 4-pounder cannonball found in March, on the eve of the battle's 190th anniversary, and a 6-pounder cannonball found in June.

Photos show archaeologists carefully cleaning the newly discovered cannonballs, which appear heavily weathered and discolored.

The Battle of the Alamo was one of the most important events in Texas history.

EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH

The engagement lasted from Feb. 23 to March 6, 1836. It saw Texian forces — including Davy Crockett and William B. Travis — hold off a much larger Mexican army.

The 13-day siege ended with Mexican troops overrunning the Texian defenders, a loss that became a rallying cry for the Texas Revolution.

The discoveries raise a question: Which army fired the cannonballs?

Lindley of the Alamo Trust told Fox News Digital the answer is a bit complicated.

"We have a good idea [of] three of the cannonballs … They were bronze cannonballs, and that was a type of material used by the Mexican army, so they may have originated with the Mexican army," she said.

She noted, however, that the cannonballs could have been picked up by the Alamo's defenders or others before the battle, so either side may have used them.

Determining whether the cannonballs were connected to the battle is more straightforward.

Lindley said archaeologists can link the artifacts to the battle through several lines of evidence, including the layers of soil in which they were found, plus other objects recovered nearby.

The same soil deposit contained musket balls and gun parts, while its depth suggested the artifacts were older than others found in layers above it.

Lindley said historians helped archaeologists determine that the cannonballs were likely found near a Mexican cannon position outside the Alamo.

"They would have been shooting toward the church in this area," she said.

Lindley, who said she was unaware of any solid cannonballs previously found at the site, attributed the recent discoveries largely to the size of the excavation area.

"We have a very large area that we're excavating. And whenever you are digging more, you have more of a chance to find more artifacts," she said.

For Lindley, the discovery also puts a tangible piece of the 1836 battle into the hands of modern-day archaeologists.

"Now we have a physical piece of evidence of the sacrifice" made here by those who lived during the battle, she said — "and their memories [have] lived on."

item.title: MATT CALKINS: After years of threats and intimidation, the bullies in the women's sports debate finally lost
item.description: Riley Gaines and advocates faced years of harassment, but Initiative 638 and Prop 134 passed in deep-blue Washington and Colorado nonetheless.
item.content:encoded:
They passed. First, Initiative 638 in Washington. Then, Prop 134 in Colorado.

Two measures that will enforce the separation of boys and girls in sports — two measures that show common sense can prevail over partisanship.

Many will view these results as a bellwether for where the rest of the country is heading. If policies like these can pass in deep-blue states, proponents will argue they can pass anywhere.

WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS APPEAR TO PASS FIRST-EVER BALLOT MEASURE SEPARATING BOYS AND GIRLS SPORTS

But me? I see something else entirely. I see the people finally sticking it to the bullies.

Let's go back to July, when Washington high school student Ahnaleigh Wilson attended a rally supporting Fever guard Sophie Cunningham at Climate Pledge Arena. Do you remember what happened inside the venue after the game started? Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton approached Wilson — who was holding a sign reading "Thank You Sophie For Speaking Up For Girls!" — and began cursing her out.

"You're f---ing insane," she allegedly said. "I hope Jesus can forgive you."

Wilson was brought to tears...but this was hardly a one-off.

HOSTILE VALKYRIES FANS VERBALLY ATTACKED WOMEN'S SPORTS ACTIVISTS AT WNBA FINALS GAME 1 IN SAN FRANCISCO

Fellow Washingtonian Frances Staudt chose not to play against a male in a high school basketball game over two years ago. Since then, she said she has endured daily harassment at Tumwater High, with people telling her they hope she chokes and dies and goes to hell. Former high school softball star Kendall Kotzmacher may have had it worse. At a Cunningham rally in Minnesota earlier this year, a pro-trans counterprotester told her that she should have been aborted.

And don't for a minute think this stops with the kids. XX-XY Athletics founder Jennifer Sey shared a video of her and her friends being called to the concourse to meet with security at a Golden State Valkyries game last month. During their march up the stairs, a woman flipped her the bird and told her to "f---ing kill yourself." But that was just a foreshock to what women's sports advocates endured at a Portland Thorns game two Fridays ago.

After a group of about 20 XX-XY supporters unfurled a banner that said "Save Women's Sports," Thorns supporters started yelling "f--- you" before sending one woman tumbling over two rows of seats. They also started poking women with flagpoles they'd brought into the stadium. I saw this up close while reporting for OutKick, but had my phone knocked out of my hand and beer poured on me while filming it.

So who got kicked out? Not the assaulters. Nope, it was the peaceful Save Women's Sports crowd — with Seattle-based podcaster Brandi Kruse having her hand restrained behind her back as she was walked up to the concourse.

BRANDI KRUSE TELLS LAURA INGRAHAM ABOUT BEING FORCED OUT OF PORTLAND SOCCER GAME: 'WE DID NOTHING WRONG'

Even a Lyft driver got in on the hazing, as he booted four XX-XY shirt-wearers from his car once he found out who they were aligned with. The bullies are everywhere.

But you know what? They lost.

People don't have to be afraid to take a pro female stance on this issue anymore. The outrage mob may try to sink their talons into anyone who does, but they've been declawed by the will of the people — who sliced right through the propaganda.

Did you know opponents of Prop 134 outspent the 'yes' campaign nearly 18 to 1—dropping $4.9 million against just $270,000—only to come up empty? Did you see all those ads or newspaper endorsements in Washington claiming that I-638 was going to lead to "invasive genital exams?"

Nobody bought it. The two measures sailed through in two of the bluer states in the country.

Just less than a month ago, I was at a cross country meet where a boy who switched to the girls team midseason was competing. Out of maybe 100 parents I tried to talk with, just two went on the record — and the vast majority refused to even be quoted anonymously.

Said one father: "I don't want my house burned down."

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

The bullies have been throwing blows on this issue for years now. Just ask advocates such as Riley Gaines, who's been enduring them from every angle.

The thing about bullies, though, is they always feel small inside. After these two measures passed, they feel even smaller.

item.title: MLW's Killer Kross faces biggest challenge yet as he defends world title against Josh Bishop at major PPV
item.description: Killer Kross says retaining his MLW World Heavyweight Championship against Josh Bishop at Saturday Night SuperFight comes down to toughness.
item.content:encoded:
Killer Kross will enter Major League Wrestling’s (MLW) Saturday Night SuperFight having to defend his MLW World Heavyweight Championship against Josh Bishop, who is riding a wave of momentum going into the pay-per-view.

Kross and Bishop will meet in a Last Man Standing match at Cicero Stadium in Chicago. It will be Bishop’s best chance at dethroning Kross, who has been the champion since Battle Riot VIII.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

"I think I’ve got a very good chance to retain," Kross told OutKick Dropkick. "However, I think it's gonna come down to who's gonna come out of this the toughest. If you're not coming in, as close to bulletproof as possible, I don't think we're gonna be able to walk out the winner on this one. Last man standing, you know what I mean? It's. This isn't about wrestling ability, this isn't about technical prowess. This is gonna be who's tougher. That's just the way I see it."

Last Man Standing matches turn out to be one of the more brutal showcases in pro wrestling.

The object is to do enough damage to your opponent that he is on his back for at least 10 seconds. Kross, himself, is coming off a title defense against Donovan Dijak on the go-home episode of "Fusion." Bishop and Dijak broke apart and Bishop delivered an Exit 187 to Dijak, seemingly building momentum to the championship fight.

MLW'S COURT BAUER TOUTS 'HUGE YEAR' FOR COMPANY AMID MEDIA DEALS, SPLASH MOVES

But that was just a part of Kross’ 2026. He admitted the year has been "painful" but also highly successful.

"I never doubted it," he said of the success he’s had this year. "But with pro wrestling, it doesn't matter really what you're capable of or what you think you can do and oftentimes, it doesn't even matter, depending on what company you're in, what sort of connection you have with the audience, if they don't want to give you the time to go out there and shine, then it's kind of like it doesn't exist.

"So, tthe only thing that was up in the air was like once I get out here, are those opportunities gonna be available because I'm ready to deliver? And they have been in mass quantity. So, I mean, it's, I'm having the time of my life. I can't say it enough, man. I really, truly am."

Despite the feud between Kross and Bishop this year, Kross recognized how far Bishop has come in his growth as a pro wrestler.

"He has a bright future ahead of him," Kross said. "I've said it before and I'll say it again, he's a perfect throwback. He's got that Sid Justice, Sid Vicious type of demeanor, and people love that, and you just can't find those types of wrestlers sitting around anymore.

"A lot of what we see in the programming is this incredible hybrid Lucia type stuff. The era of the big man is kind of few and far in between, and I think with wrestling being best formatted as a variety act, you gotta have somebody like that on the show. You need some, you need some heavy hitters, those larger than life type characters, and I definitely think he fits the bill."

Saturday Night SuperFight takes place this weekend and can be seen on Veeps at 8 p.m. ET.

item.title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to higher stroke risk, study finds
item.description: A study of nearly 450,000 adults found that both casual and heavy marijuana users faced higher odds of stroke and cardiovascular disease than non-users.
item.content:encoded:
A new study of nearly 450,000 American adults links cannabis use to an increased risk of stroke and cardiovascular disease.

The findings, scheduled for presentation at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago Nov. 6–9, show that both casual and heavy marijuana users have higher odds of heart conditions compared to non-users.

Researchers analyzed survey responses collected between 2020 and 2024 through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System.

SHARON STONE'S TERRIFYING WEED WITHDRAWAL SPARKS WARNING ABOUT TODAY'S POTENT MARIJUANA

People who reported using cannabis between one and five days per month had 23% higher odds of reporting a history of cardiovascular disease than non-users. Those using it 16 to 30 days per month had 21% higher odds.

"This study raises important concerns about cannabis use and cardiovascular health, particularly stroke," Dr. Kristen "Nicke" Worth, an Ohio-based physician and medical adviser at NuggMD, a telehealth platform for medical marijuana evaluations, told Fox News Digital.

"One finding I found particularly interesting was that people who used cannabis just one to five days per month had somewhat higher reported odds of a previous stroke than people who used it more frequently," added Worth, who was not involved in the study.

Low-frequency users had 40% higher odds of a reported stroke, while heavy users had 25% higher odds. The study found no statistically significant link between cannabis use and heart attacks.

MARIJUANA USERS MAY FACE HIDDEN DRIVING DANGER THAT STANDARD TESTS CAN MISS

"That isn't what we'd necessarily expect from a straightforward dose-response relationship, where greater exposure is associated with greater risk. But we shouldn't interpret this as evidence that heavier use is safer," Worth said.

The method of consumption did not change the outcome. Whether participants smoked, vaped or consumed edibles like gummies, the risk remained consistent, according to the researchers.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward," said lead author Dr. Aabha Divya, an assistant professor of cardiothoracic surgery at Tulane University School of Medicine, in an AHA press release.

"We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease."

The study comes amid growing commercial availability and use of the drug across the country. According to the research team, about one in six adults reported past-month cannabis use in 2024, up from one in 10 in 2020 — a 51% increase over four years.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Dr. Robert L. Page II, a professor of clinical pharmacy at the University of Colorado and an American Heart Association volunteer expert who was not involved in the study, said the findings challenge common assumptions about the drug's safety.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case," Page said in a press release.

"Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events."

Page added that doctors should question patients about marijuana use just as they do with cigarettes and alcohol.

Researchers noted several key limitations to the findings. Because the study was observational and captured data from only a single point in time, it can only show a statistical link and cannot prove that cannabis causes heart disease or strokes.

The data also relied on telephone surveys, leaving room for errors in participants' memory regarding their medical diagnoses and drug use. Additionally, the researchers did not track product strength, THC potency or total amounts consumed.

The findings remain preliminary until vetted through the full, peer-reviewed publication process.

"For patients, I wouldn't recommend making abrupt treatment decisions based on one preliminary study, but I wouldn't dismiss these findings," Worth said. "People should not discontinue prescribed cardiovascular medications because of this report."

"Anyone using cannabis, medically or recreationally, should discuss their cardiovascular history, existing risk factors, medications and treatment alternatives with their healthcare professional," she added.

item.title: Ex-MIT professor wins $6M after sex claims wrecked career, accuser joked about ‘#hetoo’
item.description: David Sabatini's $6 million defamation win over Kristin Knouse now faces cross-appeals as both sides prepare to battle in Massachusetts courts.
item.content:encoded:
A Massachusetts jury awarded former MIT biologist Dr. David Sabatini a $6 million defamation victory over sexual misconduct claims, setting the stage for cross-appeals as both legal teams prepare to take the case to a higher court.

Dr. Kristin Knouse, the former colleague whose sexual misconduct allegations dismantled Sabatini's American academic career, is challenging the October verdict. Her decision triggered a battle over legal consequences surrounding workplace misconduct claims and the authority of campus tribunals.

Knouse’s attorney, Ellen Zucker, believes that the $6 million verdict could potentially stop female scientists from reporting misconduct, claiming the jury's decision reflects a society that refuses to believe women who challenge powerful men.

US OLYMPIC HERO NANCY HOGSHEAD WINS LEGAL BATTLE AFTER VOLLEYBALL COACH'S $250M DEFAMATION SUIT IS DISMISSED

"When someone can get sued for having spoken out, that kills the willingness of anyone to participate in an investigation," Zucker told Fox News Digital. "Daring to speak out will get you sued, [and] the likelihood that anyone would come forward goes down a lot."

Sabatini’s legal team rejected the narrative. His attorney, Lisa G. Arrowood, told Fox News Digital that the verdict poses zero threat to genuine victims.

"The jury verdict in this case should have no impact on women who truly have been harassed or abused and decide to report the misconduct," Arrowood said.

"What the jury found here, based on the contemporaneous documents written by Dr. Knouse herself, was that no harassment ever occurred and that her claims of harassment and rape were false and defamatory. This jury verdict, therefore, has no bearing on people who report truthfully."

Arrowood also expressed confidence that the $6 million penalty would withstand appeal.

"This is her right," Arrowood said. "However, the judge was very careful in this case and frequently ruled in her favor on many close calls. We think her appeal will be unsuccessful."

FORMER CAL SOFTBALL PLAYER FILES LAWSUIT AGAINST UNIVERSITY, FEMALE EX-COACH OVER ALLEGED SEXUAL MISCONDUCT

Zucker argued that the verdicts will not stand, warning that penalizing accusers threatens future institutional investigations.

"We do not believe the verdicts will stand," Zucker said. "Our client came to court and told the truth about her experiences with Sabatini, as did multiple other women; investigators uncovered several violations of institutional policy."

The upcoming appellate fight will scrutinize the events that led to the lawsuit.

The pair first met in 2012, when Knouse was a doctoral student in the Harvard-MIT M.D./Ph.D. program and Sabatini served on her thesis committee. By 2018 — after Knouse had been named a Whitehead Fellow — they began a relationship, according to court documents.

FORMER UCLA GYNECOLOGIST SENTENCED AFTER PLEADING GUILTY TO SEXUALLY ASSAULTING PATIENTS AT SCHOOL

Sabatini maintained the relationship was consensual. Knouse alleged it was coerced and that Sabatini created an inappropriate workplace dynamic. A 2021 Whitehead investigation found Sabatini violated its workplace relationship policy.

Text messages made public during the case showed Knouse wrote that she would "fixate on how I’m being held as a backup and competed against other women," Boston 25 News reported.

In one message about visiting Sabatini's hotel room one night on a work retreat, she wrote: "In hindsight, it was quite aggressive, #hetoo," according to the outlet.

Knouse launched a campaign against Sabatini that she called "Covert Operation Dethrone," Boston 25 reported, and joked in one message about buying a "Lambo" if she won a settlement.

"Dr. Sabatini and his legal team do not criticize the MeToo movement or the right of women to complain of harassment," Arrowood added. "This case is unique in that the jury found that Dr. Knouse’s claims were fabricated and designed to cause harm to Dr. Sabatini."

After Knouse accused him of sexual misconduct, MIT administrators stripped Sabatini of his tenured position. The Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) dismissed him. The Whitehead Institute ousted him.

CBS NEWS FACES $20M DEFAMATION LAWSUIT AFTER MISIDENTIFYING MARYLAND TEENAGER IN REFLECTING POOL REPORT

Arrowood said that Sabatini’s team is launching its own counter-offensive on appeal, seeking to overturn the court’s earlier decision that dismissed the Whitehead Institute from the lawsuit.

MIT and HHMI were not defendants in the defamation lawsuit.

MIT declined to comment but referred Fox News Digital to a letter sent out to staff in 2022, when Sabatini resigned and the school said he was found to have "behaved in ways incompatible with the responsibilities of faculty membership."

HHMI did not respond to a request for comment.

BIDEN OFFICIALS CIRCUMVENTED COURT ORDER IN TITLE IX CASES, INCLUDING MALES IN GIRLS’ SPORTS, DOCS SHOW

The universities based their firings on internal Title IX investigations, which concluded that Sabatini violated policies by entering into an undisclosed romantic relationship with a junior researcher.

The campus tribunals require a low burden of proof, which rarely allows the accused to cross-examine the accuser, according to the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression.

Arrowood argued that the institutions rushed to judgment before the facts could be tested in a civil court.

"This verdict should send universities the message that all the facts and documents from both sides need to be obtained and analyzed before deciding to fire someone," she said.

SEND US A TIP

"Here, the investigators and the Whitehead Institute allowed one party and her lawyers to control what evidence they received and even what they could show to Dr. Sabatini. Had the full picture been shown to the institution and to the investigators, we believe the outcome would have been different."

GOT A TIP?

When the legal battle reached a Suffolk County courtroom, the jury denied Knouse’s counterclaims of harassment and instead ordered her to pay Sabatini millions for defamation.

While Sabatini won the courtroom battle, the years-long ordeal destroyed his U.S. research operation. Activist billionaire Bill Ackman stepped in and funded a new laboratory for Sabatini in Prague, where Sabatini continues his life-saving cancer research.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"I lost everything. There was nothing left of my normal life," Sabatini previously told Boston 25 News. "I've been dreaming about this moment for all this time, but often thinking I might not make it, financially, emotionally or physically."

The case now moves to the Massachusetts appellate courts. The formal briefing schedule is pending.

item.content:encoded:
A New Hampshire school district that banned two fathers from school grounds after they wore pink "XX" wristbands opposing transgender participation in girls' sports has agreed to a federal court judgment declaring it violated the plaintiffs’ First Amendment rights.

The resolution, approved Thursday by U.S. District Judge Steven McAuliffe, ends more than two years of litigation and requires the district’s risk pool to pay $275,000 in attorneys’ fees and costs.

TRANS ATHLETES DROP LAWSUIT TO GAIN ACCESS TO GIRLS' SPORTS IN NEW HAMPSHIRE AFTER SCOTUS RULING

The judgment protects the four plaintiffs’ right to silently wear the wristbands along the sidelines, in spectator areas and in parking lots at any Bow School District sporting event. It expressly declares that the district violated their constitutional rights when it barred the wristbands at a Sept. 17, 2024, girls varsity soccer game.

"It took more than two years, but the court has recognized that what happened to us was wrong," plaintiff Kyle Fellers said in a statement reported by The Associated Press.

Fellers said the ban kept him from attending half of his daughter’s soccer games during her senior year.

The case grew out of a game between Bow High School and Plymouth Regional High School, whose girls team included transgender player Parker Tirrell. The wristbands’ "XX" symbols referenced female chromosomes and expressed opposition to allowing biological males to compete in girls' sports.

DOJ REVIEWING PORTLAND THORNS INCIDENT SHOWING WOMEN’S SPORTS SUPPORTERS STRUCK, FORCIBLY REMOVED

School officials, accompanied by a police officer, confronted spectators over the wristbands. The confrontation escalated, the referee halted play and Fellers and Anthony "Andy" Foote subsequently received no-trespass orders.

Fox News Digital previously reported on Foote’s ban after he wore the wristband to his daughter’s game.

Fellers, Foote, Nicole Foote and grandfather Eldon Rash brought the lawsuit with representation from the Institute for Free Speech and local attorney Richard J. Lehmann.

Under the settlement, Primex, the district’s risk pool, will pay $225,000 to the institute and $50,000 to Lehmann Major List PLLC. Each plaintiff will receive an additional $17.91, an amount the institute said symbolizes 1791, when the First Amendment was ratified.

School officials had defended their response as an effort to protect students from harassment. Before the game, officials received reports about possible heckling and communications they believed suggested the protest could escalate. The fathers testified that they did not intend to harass or target the player.

The parents initially suffered a setback when McAuliffe denied their request for a preliminary injunction in April 2025.

But the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals concluded Aug. 26 that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claim of viewpoint discrimination and sent the case back for further proceedings.

The appeals court found no evidence the silent protest caused a material disruption before school officials intervened. It also found no evidence that any player actually saw the wristbands.

The plaintiffs "did not march, shout, chant, or otherwise disrupt the game," the court wrote, concluding their conduct "fell short of harassment and disruption."

The panel also pointed to administrators’ descriptions of the message as exclusionary or hateful as evidence that officials likely punished the spectators because they disagreed with their views.

Thursday’s resolution is a stipulated judgment agreed to by the parties. The settlement contains a provision denying wrongdoing except as expressly established in the judgment, which declares the district’s wristband ban unconstitutional.

The judgment binds the district, its Board of Education and their successors. It remains effective even if the district revises its conduct policies or athletics handbook, and the court retains authority to enforce it and the settlement.

The Associated Press reported that an attorney for the district did not respond to its request for comment.

The Institute for Free Speech said the order arrived in time for a Bow girls varsity soccer playoff game scheduled for Friday, Nov. 6.

item.title: Giants honor Rachel Apa after New York City Marathon death at age 24: 'She's in God's hands now'

item.content:encoded:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh put football on hold during his media session Wednesday, paying tribute to Rachel Apa, the 24-year-old runner who collapsed and died during Sunday's New York City Marathon.

Before taking a single question, Harbaugh addressed the tragedy directly on behalf of the entire Giants organization.

"First of all, I just want to express our thoughts and prayers to the family of Rachel Apa, a 24-year-old young athlete who passed away in the New York City Marathon this past weekend," Harbaugh said.
